lessons.title: Forces and Motion — The Basics
lessons.description: Free-body diagrams, resultant forces, Newton's three laws and weight vs mass.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Force?

A force is a push or a pull. Forces are measured in newtons (N) and they always arise from an interaction between two objects. Every time one object exerts a force on another, the second object exerts an equal force back — forces never exist alone.

Forces can be contact forces (friction, tension, normal contact force, air resistance) or non-contact forces (gravity, magnetism, electrostatic attraction). Both types are vector quantities — they have size and direction.

Key Fact

Newton's third law states that when two objects interact, they exert forces on each other that are equal in size, opposite in direction, and the same type of force. These forces act on different objects — they never cancel each other out on the same object.

Weight and the Gravitational Field

Weight is a force — the gravitational pull on an object. It is proportional to mass and is calculated using:

$$W = mg$$

where \(W\) is weight in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(g\) is the gravitational field strength in N/kg. Near Earth's surface, \(g \approx 10\) N/kg.

Mass is a measure of how much matter an object contains. It does not change with location. A student with a mass of 60 kg has that same mass whether on Earth, the Moon or in deep space. Their weight, however, changes with location: on Earth \(W = 60 \times 10 = 600\) N; on the Moon, where \(g \approx 1.6\) N/kg, \(W = 60 \times 1.6 = 96\) N.

Weight is measured using a Newton meter (spring balance). Mass is measured using a balance that compares against known masses — this works even in reduced gravity because both sides are equally affected.

Resultant Force

When several forces act on an object, their combined effect can be described by a single resultant force. If forces act in the same direction, they add together. If they act in opposite directions, the smaller is subtracted from the larger — the resultant acts in the direction of the larger force.

Key Fact

If the resultant force is zero, the object is in equilibrium: it stays still or moves at constant velocity. If the resultant force is non-zero, the object accelerates in the direction of the resultant force.

A free body diagram represents all the forces acting on one object. Each force is drawn as an arrow starting from the object, pointing in the direction the force acts. The length of each arrow is proportional to the force's size.

Example: a book resting on a table has two forces — its weight acting downwards and the normal contact force from the table acting upwards. If these are equal in size, the resultant is zero and the book stays still. Newton's insight is that this is no coincidence: the book pushes the table down; the table pushes the book up — a Newton's third law pair.

Newton's Laws in Action

Newton's first law: if the resultant force on an object is zero, its velocity does not change. A moving object at zero resultant force keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction — it does not slow down without a force acting on it. This was a profound insight: before Newton (and Galileo before him), many believed a force was needed simply to keep an object moving.

Newton's second law: the acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass:

$$F = ma$$

where \(F\) is the resultant force in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(a\) is acceleration in m/s\(^2\). A larger force produces a greater acceleration; a larger mass requires a greater force to produce the same acceleration.

A 900 kg car has a driving force of 3600 N and experiences 900 N of friction. Calculate the acceleration.

Step 1: Resultant force = 3600 − 900 = 2700 N (in the direction of motion)

Step 2: \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{2700}{900} = 3\) m/s\(^2\)

Always find the resultant force first before substituting into \(F = ma\).

Inertial mass is formally defined as the ratio \(m = F/a\) — how difficult it is to accelerate an object. A heavy truck has far greater inertia than a bicycle: the same resultant force produces much less acceleration. Newton's discovery that this same quantity governs both resistance to acceleration and gravitational attraction (weight) is one of the great connections in physics — a striking example of creative scientific thinking (IaS3).
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Newton's third law questions, always identify the two objects in the interaction and state the force pair explicitly — for example, “the Earth pulls the skydiver down with gravity; the skydiver pulls the Earth up with an equal gravitational force.” The common mistake is confusing Newton's third law pairs (on different objects) with balanced forces (on the same object). For \(F = ma\) calculations, always calculate the resultant force first — many students substitute the driving force without subtracting friction, and lose marks. Free body diagrams should always label the type of force (weight, normal contact, friction) not just the direction.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Forces are vector quantities arising from interactions between pairs of objects. Newton's third law: the two forces in an interaction pair are equal in size, opposite in direction, the same type, and act on different objects.
  • Weight \(W = mg\) depends on gravitational field strength; mass does not change with location. Resultant force determines whether an object accelerates. If resultant force is zero, the object is in equilibrium.
  • \(F = ma\): greater force → greater acceleration; greater mass → smaller acceleration for the same force. Free body diagrams summarise all forces on one object and help find the resultant.

practice_questions.text: State Newton's third law of motion. Give one example of a Newton's third law force pair.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: when two objects interact, they exert forces on each other that are equal in size, opposite in direction and the same type / act on different objects.
1 mark: a valid example, e.g. a book pushes down on a table (contact force); the table pushes up on the book with an equal contact force — accept any correct pair identifying the two objects and directions.

practice_questions.text: A cyclist of mass 70 kg, including the bicycle, experiences a driving force of 280 N from pedalling and a resistive force of 80 N from air resistance. Calculate the acceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
Resultant force = 280 − 80 = 200 N [1 mark for correct resultant]
\(a = F/m = 200/70 = 2.86\) m/s\(^2\) (accept 2.9 m/s\(^2\)) [1 mark for correct answer with unit].

Common error: using 280 N rather than the resultant force.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between mass and weight, using an example to illustrate your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states mass is measured in kg and weight in N.
Secure: mass is the amount of matter in an object; it does not change with location, measured in kg. Weight is the gravitational force on an object; it depends on the gravitational field strength at that location, measured in N.
Mastering: as Secure, plus gives a numerical example (e.g. a 50 kg student weighs 500 N on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) but only 80 N on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg); their mass remains 50 kg).

[1 mark: mass = amount of matter, kg, does not change; 1 mark: weight = gravitational force, N, depends on location; 1 mark: valid numerical example]

practice_questions.text: Draw a labelled free body diagram for a skydiver falling at terminal velocity. Use your diagram to explain why the skydiver is not accelerating.
practice_questions.marks:
Diagram [2 marks]: two arrows from the skydiver — weight downward, labelled W (or weight, or mg); drag/air resistance upward, labelled F_drag (or air resistance); both arrows equal in length.

Explanation [2 marks]: the resultant force is zero because weight equals air resistance; by Newton's first law / Newton's second law with F = 0, acceleration = 0, so the skydiver falls at constant (terminal) velocity.

Emerging: draws arrows but does not label or explain.
Mastering: links explicitly to F = ma with F_resultant = 0 → a = 0.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Newton's discovery of the universal nature of gravity — that the same force causes objects to fall on Earth and keeps the Moon in orbit — is considered an important example of creative thinking in science.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states Newton connected Earth's gravity to the Moon's orbit.
Secure: before Newton, these were considered unrelated phenomena; Newton's insight (IaS3) was to propose that the same mathematical law — gravity decreasing with distance squared — could explain both falling apples and planetary orbits; this required imagination beyond what the observations alone suggested.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that good scientific ideas go beyond the data and make testable predictions; Newton's law correctly predicted the orbits of other planets and eventually led to the discovery of Neptune through orbital anomalies — demonstrating how a creative model can generate new science.

[1 mark: identifies what Newton connected; 1 mark: explains why it required imagination/creativity; 1 mark: notes the law makes testable predictions; 1 mark: gives a specific consequence (e.g. planetary orbit prediction); 1 mark: links to how models in science develop with evidence (IaS3)]

practice_questions.text:
A crate of mass 120 kg is pushed along a flat surface by a force of 360 N. It moves at constant velocity.
(a) What is the resultant force on the crate?
(b) Calculate the friction force acting on the crate.
(c) If the pushing force increases to 480 N while friction stays the same, calculate the new acceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Zero [1 mark] — constant velocity means no acceleration, so resultant force = 0 (Newton's first law).

(b) If resultant = 0, friction = driving force = 360 N [1 mark].

(c) Resultant = 480 − 360 = 120 N [1 mark]
\(a = F/m = 120/120 = 1\) m/s\(^2\) [1 mark for calculation, 1 mark for correct unit].

Emergng: correctly answers (a) only.
Secure: correctly answers all three with working shown.
Mastering: explicitly justifies (a) with Newton's first law and links friction = 360 N to equilibrium argument. [1 mark for clear logical justification in (a)/(b)]

glossary_terms.definition: A push or pull arising from an interaction between two objects, measured in newtons (N).
Forces that act between objects in direct physical contact, such as friction, tension and normal contact force.
Forces that act between objects without physical contact, such as gravity, magnetism and electrostatic attraction.
The force acting on an object due to gravity, measured in newtons (N). Weight depends on where the object is located.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. Mass is the same everywhere in the universe.
A device used to measure force by the extension of a calibrated spring, also called a spring balance.
The single force that has the same effect as all the individual forces acting on an object combined.
The state of an object when the resultant force on it is zero — it is either stationary or moving at constant velocity.
A diagram showing all forces acting on a single object as labelled arrows, each arrow's length proportional to the force magnitude.
The tendency of an object to resist changes to its motion — defined as the ratio of the resultant force to the acceleration it produces.

lessons.title: Describing Motion — Speed, Velocity, Acceleration
lessons.description: Speed, velocity, acceleration, motion graphs, and stopping distances — including v² = u² + 2as.
lessons.content_html:
Speed and Distance

Speed tells you how fast an object is moving. It is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction. The equation for speed is:

$$v = \frac{s}{t}$$

where \(v\) is speed in m/s, \(s\) is distance in metres (m), and \(t\) is time in seconds (s). This rearranges to \(s = vt\) and \(t = s/v\).

Key Fact

Typical speeds to know: walking ≈ 1.5 m/s, running ≈ 3 m/s, cycling ≈ 6 m/s, car in town ≈ 13 m/s, car on motorway ≈ 30 m/s, train ≈ 55 m/s, sound in air ≈ 330 m/s.

Velocity and Displacement

Velocity is the vector equivalent of speed: it has both magnitude and direction. Two cars travelling at 30 m/s in opposite directions have the same speed but different velocities.

Displacement is similarly the vector equivalent of distance — it is the net distance from the starting point in a specific direction. An athlete who completes one full lap of a 400 m track has travelled 400 m (distance) but has a displacement of 0 m (they ended where they started).

Acceleration

Acceleration is how quickly an object's velocity changes. The equation is:

$$a = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

where \(a\) is acceleration in m/s\(^2\), \(v\) is final velocity in m/s, \(u\) is initial velocity in m/s, and \(t\) is time in seconds. A negative value of \(a\) means the object is decelerating.

A bus accelerates from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 seconds. Calculate the acceleration.

\(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{16 - 4}{6} = \frac{12}{6} = 2\) m/s\(^2\)

Now suppose the bus then brakes from 16 m/s to rest in 8 s: \(a = \frac{0 - 16}{8} = -2\) m/s\(^2\) (deceleration of 2 m/s\(^2\)).

Key Fact

For uniform (constant) acceleration, use:

$$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$

where \(s\) is distance travelled in metres. This equation is essential when time is not given or needed.

A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes uniformly to rest over a distance of 50 m. Calculate the deceleration.

Known: \(u = 20\) m/s, \(v = 0\) m/s, \(s = 50\) m.

\(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\)

\(0 = 400 + 2a \times 50\)

\(100a = -400\)

\(a = -4\) m/s\(^2\) (deceleration of 4 m/s\(^2\))

Time was not given and was not needed — this is exactly when \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) is the right tool.

Distance-Time Graphs

A distance-time graph shows how far an object has travelled over time. Key features: a horizontal line means stationary; a straight diagonal line means constant speed; a steepening curve means increasing speed (acceleration).

The speed at any point equals the gradient of the line: \(\text{speed} = \frac{\text{change in distance}}{\text{change in time}}\). For a straight line, pick two points far apart and divide the rise by the run. For a curve, draw a tangent at the point of interest and find its gradient.

Velocity-Time Graphs

A velocity-time graph is even more powerful. The gradient gives the acceleration. The area under the line gives the total distance travelled.

A horizontal line means constant velocity (acceleration = 0). A line sloping upward means increasing velocity (positive acceleration). A line sloping downward means decreasing velocity (deceleration). Complex shapes can be split into triangles and rectangles to find the total area (= total distance).

A common method for measuring acceleration is to use a trolley on a ramp with a light gate connected to a data logger. The independent variable is the force applied (e.g. by varying the hanging mass); the dependent variable is the acceleration. Controlled variables include the total mass of the system. The light gate measures the time taken for a card of known width to pass — from this, both speed and acceleration can be calculated. Results plotted as acceleration against force produce a straight line through the origin if \(F = ma\) holds.

Graphs and Calculations: Exam Technique

When interpreting motion graphs, look at the gradient first. A flat line on a distance-time graph means the object is stationary; a flat line on a velocity-time graph means constant velocity with zero acceleration. Steeper gradients indicate faster speed or greater acceleration. To find displacement from a velocity-time graph, calculate the area under the line — including enclosed areas between the graph line and the time axis, which represent displacement in a particular direction. A common exam error is confusing the gradient, which gives acceleration, with the area, which gives displacement, on a velocity-time graph.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error in motion calculations is choosing the wrong equation. Use \(a = (v - u)/t\) when time is given; use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) when time is absent. For graph questions: on a distance-time graph, gradient = speed; on a velocity-time graph, gradient = acceleration and area under the line = distance. Always include units in your answer — marks are awarded specifically for correct units. When describing motion from a graph, describe each distinct section separately (e.g. “from 0 to 5 s the object accelerates uniformly; from 5 to 10 s it travels at constant velocity”).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Speed (scalar) and velocity (vector) both measure how fast an object moves; velocity includes direction. Displacement (vector) measures net distance and direction from start to finish. Acceleration = rate of change of velocity = \((v - u) / t\).
  • On a distance-time graph, gradient = speed. On a velocity-time graph, gradient = acceleration and area under the line = distance travelled.
  • For uniform acceleration without time: use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). This is the equation to reach for when a question gives initial speed, final speed and distance — but not time.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between speed and velocity. Give an example to illustrate your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: speed is a scalar quantity (magnitude only); velocity is a vector quantity (magnitude and direction).
1 mark: valid example, e.g. a car travelling at 20 m/s north has the same speed as one travelling at 20 m/s south, but different velocities.

practice_questions.text: A sprinter accelerates from rest to 9 m/s in 1.5 s. Calculate the acceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
\(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{9 - 0}{1.5} = 6\) m/s\(^2\)

1 mark for correct substitution.
1 mark for correct answer with unit (m/s\(^2\)).

practice_questions.text:
A velocity-time graph shows a straight line from (0 s, 0 m/s) to (10 s, 30 m/s), then a horizontal line from (10 s, 30 m/s) to (20 s, 30 m/s).
(a) Calculate the acceleration in the first 10 seconds.
(b) Calculate the total distance travelled in 20 seconds.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(a = \frac{30 - 0}{10} = 3\) m/s\(^2\) [1 mark]

(b) Distance in first 10 s = area under triangle = \(\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 30 = 150\) m [1 mark]
Distance in next 10 s = area under rectangle = \(10 \times 30 = 300\) m [1 mark]
Total = 150 + 300 = 450 m [1 mark]

Common error: using \(v \times t\) for the first section instead of finding the area of a triangle.

practice_questions.text: A train enters a station at 25 m/s and decelerates uniformly to rest. The braking distance is 625 m. Calculate the deceleration.
practice_questions.marks:
Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\):
\(0 = 25^2 + 2a \times 625\)
\(0 = 625 + 1250a\)
\(1250a = -625\)
\(a = -0.5\) m/s\(^2\) (deceleration of 0.5 m/s\(^2\)) [4 marks: 1 for equation, 1 for correct substitution, 1 for rearrangement, 1 for answer + unit]

Note: time was not given — \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) is the appropriate equation.

practice_questions.text: Describe how you could use a ramp, trolley and light gate to investigate how acceleration depends on the resultant force. Identify the independent, dependent and one control variable.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: names equipment without linking to variables.
Secure:
- Independent variable: resultant force (varied by changing hanging mass on a pulley).
- Dependent variable: acceleration (measured from light gate timing data).
- Control variable: total mass of trolley + masses kept constant.
- Method: release trolley from rest; light gate records time for known-width card to pass through two gates; calculate speed at each gate; acceleration = change in speed ÷ time between gates (or use data logger). Repeat for different forces; plot acceleration vs force.

[1 mark: independent variable correctly identified with method; 1 mark: dependent variable correctly identified; 1 mark: valid control variable; 1 mark: clear method showing how acceleration is actually measured]

practice_questions.text: Scientists use mathematical models to predict the motion of moving objects. Explain, using the equations of motion as an example, how mathematical models in science can be useful and what their limitations might be.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states models are used to make predictions.
Secure: the equations of motion (e.g. \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\)) are a simple mathematical model — they can predict the speed and position of an object if acceleration is known and constant; this has real applications in transport engineering and spacecraft design.
Limitations: the model assumes uniform (constant) acceleration — in reality, air resistance and engine force change as speed changes, so the model breaks down for objects accelerating over long distances or at high speeds.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that models are always tested against real measurements; when predictions match observations closely, the model is said to be valid, but a single clear discrepancy can expose a limitation and prompt model refinement (IaS3).

[1 mark: model can predict speed/position given initial conditions; 1 mark: real application; 1 mark: identifies assumption of uniform acceleration; 1 mark: explains when this breaks down; 1 mark: links to testing models against data / IaS3]

glossary_terms.definition: How fast an object is moving — the distance it travels per unit time. Speed is a scalar quantity, measured in m/s.
Speed in a specified direction — a vector quantity measured in m/s.

lessons.title: Energy in Motion — Crumple Zones and Momentum
lessons.description: Kinetic energy, GPE, momentum, stopping distances and why crumple zones save lives.
lessons.content_html:
Energy in Moving Objects

Whenever an object moves, it stores energy in its kinetic energy store. The equation is:

$$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$

where \(E_k\) is kinetic energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(v\) is speed in m/s. Notice that speed is squared — doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy, which is why fast driving is so much more dangerous than slow driving.

Key Fact

Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed. Double the speed → four times the kinetic energy. This means braking distance also increases with the square of speed — twice as fast means four times the distance to stop with the same braking force.

Gravitational Potential Energy

When an object is raised above the ground, work is done against gravity and energy is stored as gravitational potential energy (GPE):

$$E_{gpe} = mgh$$

where \(m\) is mass in kg, \(g\) is gravitational field strength (approximately 10 N/kg near Earth), and \(h\) is height in metres. When the object falls, GPE transfers to kinetic energy (assuming no friction or air resistance).

A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Calculate its speed just before it hits the ground. (Ignore air resistance.)

GPE at top = \(mgh = 2 \times 10 \times 5 = 100\) J

By conservation of energy: \(E_k = 100\) J

\(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 100 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times v^2 = 100 \Rightarrow v^2 = 100 \Rightarrow v = 10\) m/s

Stopping Distances and Road Safety

When a vehicle needs to stop suddenly, the total stopping distance has two components:

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance

Thinking distance increases linearly with speed (higher speed → more distance covered in the same reaction time). Factors that increase thinking distance: tiredness, alcohol or drugs, distractions. Braking distance increases with the square of speed (because kinetic energy ∝ v²). Factors that increase braking distance: worn tyres or brakes, wet or icy roads, greater vehicle mass or speed.

Key Fact

Large decelerations during sudden braking generate very large forces on vehicle occupants (\(F = ma\), large negative \(a\) → large \(F\)). These forces can cause serious injury — which is why reducing deceleration time is the key principle behind vehicle safety features.

Momentum

Every moving object has momentum. The equation is:

$$p = mv$$

where \(p\) is momentum in kg m/s, \(m\) is mass in kg, and \(v\) is velocity in m/s. Momentum is a vector — its direction is the same as the velocity.

In a closed system (no external forces), the total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after. This is called the conservation of momentum. For two objects colliding: \(m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2\).

When a vehicle collides, its momentum changes from its speed-before value to zero. This change in momentum is called the impulse:

$$\text{impulse} = F \Delta t = \Delta p$$

A crumple zone is the front or rear section of a car designed to deform (crumple) during a collision. By crumpling, the car takes longer to come to rest — the time over which momentum changes (\(\Delta t\)) increases. Since \(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\), a longer time means a smaller force on the passengers for the same momentum change.

This is the precise chain of reasoning you must reproduce in an exam: crumple zone deforms → collision time increases → same momentum change occurs over a longer time → average force on occupants is reduced → injury risk is lower. Saying crumple zones “absorb force” or “act as a barrier” misses the physics and will not earn full marks.

The same principle applies to airbags (increase contact time between driver and steering wheel), seatbelts (stretch slightly to extend stopping time), cycle helmets and padded sports equipment.

Conservation of Momentum: Worked Example

Consider two trolleys: trolley A (2 kg, moving at 3 m/s) collides with stationary trolley B (1 kg) and they stick together. Total momentum before = 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s. After: (2 + 1) x v = 6, so v = 2 m/s. Kinetic energy before = 9 J; after = 6 J. The 3 J difference converts to thermal energy and sound, making this an inelastic collision. In a perfectly elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved, a distinction the examiner often tests.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The crumple zone question is one of the most frequently lost marks in this topic. You must include all steps: the crumple zone extends collision time (\(\Delta t\) increases); for the same change in momentum (\(\Delta p\)), a larger \(\Delta t\) means smaller average force (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\)). Simply writing “it absorbs the impact” or “it reduces the force” without the time-extension reasoning earns no marks. For kinetic energy calculations, always substitute before squaring: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2\) — a common mistake is to forget the \(\frac{1}{2}\). For momentum conservation, be careful with directions — assign positive/negative signs to velocities moving in opposite directions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Kinetic energy \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\) grows with the square of speed — doubling speed quadruples KE and braking distance. GPE = \(mgh\) transfers to KE as an object falls (conservation of energy).
  • Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Large decelerations cause large forces (\(F = ma\)), which is why sudden stops can injure passengers.
  • Momentum \(p = mv\) is conserved in collisions. Crumple zones extend collision time, reducing the average force on occupants for the same change in momentum (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\)).

practice_questions.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s.
practice_questions.marks:
\(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 1500 \times 400 = 300{,}000\) J (300 kJ)

1 mark for correct substitution into \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).
1 mark for correct answer with unit (J or kJ).

Common error: forgetting the \(\frac{1}{2}\) factor, giving 600,000 J.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the relationship between force, change in momentum and time, why crumple zones at the front of a car reduce the risk of injury in a collision.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states crumple zones reduce the force.
Secure: crumple zone deforms during the collision, increasing the time over which momentum changes (\(\Delta t\) increases); since \(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\) and momentum change is the same, a greater \(\Delta t\) means a smaller average force on the occupants.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that this reduces peak deceleration and therefore peak force; links to why the crumple zone design is at the front/rear (passenger compartment is rigid to protect occupants). Correctly rejects the explanation that crumple zones “absorb force.”

[1 mark: crumple zone extends collision time; 1 mark: same \(\Delta p\) over longer \(\Delta t\) means smaller \(F\) using \(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\); 1 mark: therefore force on passengers is reduced → injury risk lower]

practice_questions.text:
A cyclist of mass 75 kg (including bicycle) is travelling at 8 m/s.
(a) Calculate the momentum of the cyclist.
(b) The cyclist brakes to a stop in 4 s. Calculate the average braking force.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(p = mv = 75 \times 8 = 600\) kg m/s [1 mark: correct calculation with unit]

(b) Change in momentum \(\Delta p = 600 - 0 = 600\) kg m/s
\(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{600}{4} = 150\) N [2 marks: 1 for identifying \(\Delta p\), 1 for correct force with unit]

Alternatively via \(F = ma\): \(a = (0 - 8)/4 = -2\) m/s\(^2\); \(F = 75 \times 2 = 150\) N ✓ [1 mark for either valid method]

practice_questions.text:
A ball of mass 0.5 kg is dropped from a height of 8 m. Calculate:
(a) The gravitational potential energy at the top.
(b) The speed of the ball just before it hits the ground. (Assume no air resistance; g = 10 N/kg.)
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(E_{gpe} = mgh = 0.5 \times 10 \times 8 = 40\) J [1 mark: correct calculation with unit]

(b) By conservation of energy: \(E_k = 40\) J
\(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 40 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times v^2 = 40 \Rightarrow 0.25v^2 = 40 \Rightarrow v^2 = 160 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{160} \approx 12.6\) m/s [3 marks: 1 for equating GPE to KE, 1 for rearrangement, 1 for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: Explain the factors that affect both the thinking distance and the braking distance of a vehicle, and discuss how Newton's laws of motion have led to improvements in road safety through the design of safety features.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: lists some factors without explanation.
Developing: identifies thinking distance factors (reaction time, speed, alcohol/drugs/distractions) and braking distance factors (speed, road surface, tyre/brake condition, mass) with brief explanation.
Secure: as Developing, plus explains the physics — braking distance ∝ v² because KE = ½mv²; stopping requires KE to be removed by work done by braking force (W = Fd); larger KE needs more braking distance; also explains crumple zones, seatbelts or airbags using the impulse/momentum principle (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\)).
Mastering: as Secure, plus evaluates the trade-off — increasing collision time reduces force but requires the car to crumple (permanent deformation is the cost); risk-benefit framing: society accepts the cost of replacing the crumple zone because the benefit (reduced injury) far outweighs it; links to IaS4 risk-benefit analysis.

[2 marks: thinking distance factors correctly explained; 2 marks: braking distance factors correctly explained with \(v^2\) link; 1 mark: safety feature explained using impulse/momentum; 1 mark: risk-benefit or Newton's law evaluation]

practice_questions.text: A 2000 kg lorry travelling at 15 m/s collides with and attaches to a stationary 500 kg car. Calculate the velocity of the combined vehicles immediately after the collision.
practice_questions.marks:
Use conservation of momentum:
Momentum before = \(m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = (2000 \times 15) + (500 \times 0) = 30{,}000\) kg m/s [1 mark]
Momentum after = \((m_1 + m_2)v = 2500v\) [1 mark]
\(2500v = 30{,}000 \Rightarrow v = \frac{30{,}000}{2500} = 12\) m/s [2 marks: 1 for equation, 1 for correct answer with unit]

Common error: not adding masses after attachment, or only using one object's momentum.

knowledge_checks.q: A car's speed doubles from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
What is the correct explanation for why a crumple zone reduces injury in a collision?
options: It absorbs force so the passenger feels nothing
It extends the collision time, reducing the average force for the same momentum change
It reduces the momentum of the vehicle
It acts as a rigid barrier between the passenger and the impact

knowledge_checks.q: Stopping distance equals thinking distance plus _____.
The equation for gravitational potential energy is \(E_{gpe}\) = _____.
Match each safety feature to the physics principle it uses:
right: Deforms to extend collision time and reduce force
Cushions impact and increases stopping time for upper body
Stretches slightly to extend deceleration time and reduce peak force

flashcard_questions.a: KE = ½mv², where m is mass in kg and v is velocity in m/s.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the equation for kinetic energy, and what do the symbols represent?

flashcard_questions.a: Egpe = mgh (energy in J, mass in kg, g in N/kg, height in m).
flashcard_questions.q: Give the equation for gravitational potential energy.

flashcard_questions.a: It quadruples — kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared.
flashcard_questions.q: If a car's speed doubles, what happens to its kinetic energy?

flashcard_questions.a: Momentum (p) = mass × velocity (p = mv), measured in kg m/s.
flashcard_questions.q: What is momentum and how is it calculated?

flashcard_questions.a: Total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after, in a closed system.
flashcard_questions.q: State the conservation of momentum principle.

flashcard_questions.a: Impulse = FΔt = Δp (impulse in N s = kg m/s).
flashcard_questions.q: Give the equation linking impulse, force and time.

flashcard_questions.a: Crumple zones extend collision time, so the same momentum change produces a smaller average force on occupants.
flashcard_questions.q: Explain the crumple zone mechanism in one sentence.

flashcard_questions.a: Thinking distance + braking distance.
flashcard_questions.q: What two components make up stopping distance?

flashcard_questions.a: Any two: higher speed, tiredness, alcohol or drugs, distractions (e.g. phone).
flashcard_questions.q: Name two factors that increase thinking distance.

flashcard_questions.a: Any two: higher speed, wet/icy road, worn brakes or tyres, greater vehicle mass.
flashcard_questions.q: Name two factors that increase braking distance.

glossary_terms.definition: The energy stored in a moving object, equal to half its mass multiplied by the square of its speed.
The energy stored in an object because of its position in a gravitational field, equal to mass × gravitational field strength × height.
The total distance travelled by a vehicle from when the driver first sees a hazard to when the vehicle comes to rest.
The distance travelled between a driver seeing a hazard and applying the brakes — depends on reaction time and speed.
The distance travelled from when the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops — increases with the square of speed.
The product of an object's mass and velocity; a vector quantity measured in kg m/s.
The principle that in a closed system, total momentum remains constant — momentum before an event equals momentum after.
The change in momentum of an object, equal to the force multiplied by the time over which the force acts.
A specially designed section of a vehicle that deforms on impact, increasing collision time and reducing the force on occupants.

lessons.title: Radioactivity and Half-Life
lessons.description: Atomic models, alpha, beta and gamma radiation, half-life calculations and nuclear equations.
lessons.content_html:
How Our Understanding of the Atom Developed

The model of the atom has changed several times as new evidence became available — a classic example of how scientific explanations develop with evidence (IaS3). Early in the 19th century, John Dalton proposed that matter is made of tiny, indivisible solid spheres. This explained chemical reactions but had no internal structure.

In the late 19th century, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and replaced Dalton's model with the plum pudding model — a positive sphere with electrons dotted through it like plums in a pudding. This was overturned in 1910–1911 when Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most particles passed straight through, but some deflected sharply and a small fraction bounced back. The only explanation was a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space.

Key Fact

The Rutherford-Geiger-Marsden alpha particle scattering experiment (published 1911) provided evidence for the nuclear model. Bohr later refined this by proposing electrons occupy fixed energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, completing the modern picture.

Atomic Structure

Every atom has a nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in energy levels. Atoms are extremely small — on the order of \(10^{-10}\) m across — and the nucleus is about a hundred-thousandth of the diameter of the whole atom.

An element is defined by its number of protons (atomic number). Different forms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes. We write isotopes in nuclear notation as \(^A_Z X\), where \(A\) is the mass number (protons + neutrons) and \(Z\) is the atomic number (protons).

Types of Radioactive Decay

Some atomic nuclei are unstable and emit radiation to become more stable — they are radioactive. Radioactive decay is a random process: you cannot predict when any particular nucleus will decay. There are four types of emission:

Alpha (\(\alpha\)) — two protons and two neutrons (a helium-4 nucleus: \(^4_2\text{He}\)). Strongly ionising; stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper. In decay, mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2.

Beta (\(\beta\)) — a high-speed electron emitted when a neutron in the nucleus converts to a proton. Moderately ionising; stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Atomic number increases by 1; mass number unchanged.

Gamma (\(\gamma\)) — high-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus after other decay. Weakly ionising; only significantly reduced by several centimetres of lead or metres of concrete. No change in mass number or atomic number.

Neutron emission — occasionally an unstable nucleus emits a neutron. Mass number decreases by 1; atomic number unchanged.

Example nuclear equation for alpha decay of radium-226: \(^{226}_{88}\text{Ra} \rightarrow ^{222}_{86}\text{Rn} + ^4_2\text{He}\). Check: top numbers balance (226 = 222 + 4) ✓; bottom numbers balance (88 = 86 + 2) ✓.

Key Fact

Ionising power and penetrating power are inversely related: alpha is most ionising, least penetrating (stopped by paper); gamma is least ionising, most penetrating (requires lead or thick concrete to reduce significantly).

Half-Life

As a radioactive sample decays, the number of unstable nuclei decreases over time, so the activity (number of decays per second) also decreases. The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for either the number of undecayed nuclei, or the activity (measured in becquerels, Bq), to halve.

After one half-life: half the original nuclei remain. After two half-lives: a quarter remain. After three half-lives: one eighth remain. The net decline can be expressed as a ratio: after \(n\) half-lives, the fraction remaining is \(\frac{1}{2^n}\). This pattern can be used to read off half-life from an activity-time graph, or to calculate the fraction remaining after a given number of half-lives.

A radioactive sample has an initial activity of 3200 Bq. After 60 days the activity is 200 Bq. Calculate the half-life.

Count the halvings: 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 → 200. That is 4 halvings.

4 half-lives = 60 days, so one half-life = \(\frac{60}{4} = 15\) days.

You can also calculate from an activity-time graph by reading off the time it takes for activity to halve at any point on the decay curve — the half-life is the same throughout (a property of exponential decay). The ratio of activity after \(n\) half-lives to the original activity is \(\frac{1}{2^n}\).

Contamination and Irradiation

Contamination means radioactive material has been deposited on or inside the body (e.g. ingested or inhaled). This is particularly dangerous because the source continues to irradiate nearby cells indefinitely until it decays or is removed. Irradiation is exposure to an external radiation source — once the source is removed, exposure stops. Alpha particles are especially dangerous if a source is inside the body (high ionising power), but outside the body they are stopped by skin and pose less risk.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For nuclear equations, always check that both the mass numbers (top) and atomic numbers (bottom) balance on each side — this is a quick way to find a missing particle. For half-life calculations, use the step-halving method (3200 → 1600 → 800 ...) to count half-lives rather than trying to use logarithms at GCSE. On activity-time graphs, the half-life can be read at any point — it should be the same wherever you measure it. A common error is confusing contamination (source inside the body — ongoing risk) with irradiation (external source — risk stops when source moves away). Questions on the development of the atomic model require you to name the scientists (Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford/Geiger/Marsden, Bohr, Chadwick) and state what evidence or discovery led to each model revision.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The atomic model developed from Dalton's solid sphere → Thomson's plum pudding → Rutherford's nuclear model (from alpha scattering, published 1911) → Bohr's energy levels. Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. Each change was driven by new experimental evidence.
  • Alpha (\(^4_2\text{He}\)), beta (electron), gamma (EM wave) and neutron emissions differ in ionising power, penetrating power and effect on the nucleus. Nuclear equations must balance mass number and atomic number on both sides.
  • Half-life is the time for activity to halve. After \(n\) half-lives, the fraction remaining is \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\). Contamination (source inside body) is more dangerous than irradiation (external source) because exposure continues after the source moves away.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between alpha particles and gamma rays.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two differences, 1 mark each:
- Alpha particles consist of two protons and two neutrons (helium nuclei); gamma rays are high-frequency electromagnetic waves (no mass or charge).
- Alpha particles are stopped by paper / a few cm of air; gamma rays require several cm of lead or metres of concrete.
- Alpha particles are strongly ionising; gamma rays are weakly ionising.
- Alpha emission reduces mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2; gamma emission does not change mass number or atomic number.

practice_questions.text: A radioactive isotope has an activity of 6400 Bq. After 80 minutes, its activity has fallen to 400 Bq. Calculate the half-life.
practice_questions.marks:
Count halvings: 6400 → 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 = 4 half-lives [1 mark]
4 half-lives = 80 minutes → half-life = \(80 / 4 = 20\) minutes [1 mark]

Common error: dividing 80 by 6400 rather than counting the halvings.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the plum pudding model of the atom was replaced by the nuclear model. Refer to the experimental evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states an experiment was done with gold foil.
Secure: the Rutherford-Geiger-Marsden experiment fired alpha particles at thin gold foil; most passed straight through (consistent with mostly empty space), but some were deflected and a few bounced straight back — this was not predicted by the plum pudding model (which assumed a diffuse positive charge and would allow all particles through with only small deflections).
Mastering: as Secure, plus explains that bouncing back required a tiny, very dense, positively charged region (nucleus) repelling the positive alpha particles — the nuclear model was proposed to fit this evidence; the model was accepted because it explained all the observations.

[1 mark: experiment correctly described (alpha particles, gold foil); 1 mark: key result described (most pass through, some deflect, few bounce back); 1 mark: explains why the plum pudding model could not account for the results and what the nuclear model proposed]

practice_questions.text:
Balance the following nuclear equation for the alpha decay of polonium-210:
\(^{210}_{84}\text{Po} \rightarrow ^{A}_{Z}\text{Pb} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}\)
State the values of A and Z.
practice_questions.marks:
A = 210 − 4 = 206 [1 mark]
Z = 84 − 2 = 82 [1 mark]

So the daughter nucleus is \(^{206}_{82}\text{Pb}\) (lead-206).

Verification: 210 = 206 + 4 ✓; 84 = 82 + 2 ✓.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between contamination by a radioactive material and irradiation by a radioactive source. In your answer, discuss how the half-life of a material affects the hazard it presents.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: distinguishes contamination (source inside body) from irradiation (external source).
Secure:
- Contamination: radioactive material deposited on or inside the body; source continues to irradiate nearby tissue even if the external source is moved away — ongoing risk.
- Irradiation: exposure to radiation from an external source; risk ceases when the source is removed.
- Half-life significance: a long half-life means slow decay, so the material remains hazardous for a long time; a very short half-life decays quickly but initially high activity poses an acute risk; in contamination, short half-life may be preferable in medical contexts (e.g. tracers) as activity decreases quickly inside the body.
Mastering: as Secure, plus discusses which radiation type is most dangerous in each context (alpha is strongly ionising inside the body — dangerous in contamination; less hazardous as irradiation because it is stopped by skin); links this to IaS4 risk-benefit analysis when making decisions about using radioactive materials in medicine.

[1 mark: contamination correctly defined; 1 mark: irradiation correctly defined and contrasted; 1 mark: explains why contamination is more hazardous; 1 mark: half-life linked to duration of hazard; 1 mark: named radiation type linked to contamination vs irradiation hazard]

practice_questions.text: A patient is given a radioactive tracer for a medical scan. The tracer has a half-life of 6 hours and an initial activity of 800 Bq. Calculate the activity after 24 hours, and explain why a short half-life is preferred for medical tracers.
practice_questions.marks:
Calculation [3 marks]:
24 hours = 4 half-lives (24 ÷ 6 = 4) [1 mark]
Fraction remaining = \((\frac{1}{2})^4 = \frac{1}{16}\) [1 mark]
Activity = \(800 \times \frac{1}{16} = 50\) Bq [1 mark]

Explanation [3 marks]:
Emerging: states a short half-life is safer.
Secure: short half-life means the tracer decays rapidly, so the patient is only exposed to significant radiation for a short time; the activity falls to safe levels quickly, reducing the total radiation dose to the patient.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes the trade-off — the half-life must be long enough for imaging to be completed before the activity falls too low (risk-benefit: IaS4); also acknowledges that gamma-emitting tracers are used because gamma rays pass out of the body for detection, while alpha emitters inside the body would cause greater cell damage due to high ionising power.

[1 mark: correct calculation of 4 half-lives; 1 mark: activity = 50 Bq; 1 mark: correct fraction remaining used; 1 mark: short half-life reduces radiation dose after scan; 1 mark: must be long enough to complete the scan — trade-off identified; 1 mark: gamma emitter preferred / alpha would be most dangerous internally]

knowledge_checks.q: What experimental evidence led to the replacement of the plum pudding model of the atom?
options: Electrons were discovered orbiting the nucleus at fixed distances
Alpha particles fired at gold foil mostly passed through, but some bounced back
X-ray images showed the nucleus is dense and positive
Neutrons were found to have no charge inside the nucleus

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of radiation is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium?
The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for its activity to fall to _____ of its original value.
In alpha decay, the mass number of the nucleus decreases by _____ and the atomic number decreases by 2.
Match each atomic model to the scientist who proposed it:
right: Dalton — atoms as tiny indivisible balls
Thomson — positive sphere with embedded electrons
Rutherford — tiny dense positive nucleus, mostly empty space

flashcard_questions.q: What is the plum pudding model of the atom?

flashcard_questions.a: The Rutherford-Geiger-Marsden alpha particle scattering experiment using thin gold foil (results published 1911).
flashcard_questions.q: What experiment provided evidence for the nuclear model of the atom?

flashcard_questions.a: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
flashcard_questions.q: What is an isotope?

flashcard_questions.q: How does alpha emission affect the nucleus?

flashcard_questions.a: Atomic number increases by 1; mass number is unchanged (a neutron converts to a proton).
flashcard_questions.q: How does beta emission affect the nucleus?

flashcard_questions.a: One eighth (½ × ½ × ½ = 1/8).
flashcard_questions.q: After 3 half-lives, what fraction of the original radioactive nuclei remain?

flashcard_questions.a: Contamination is radioactive material on or inside the body (ongoing risk); irradiation is external exposure (stops when source moves away).
flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between contamination and irradiation?

flashcard_questions.a: Alpha particles are strongly ionising and cause significant cell damage, but are stopped before reaching the body from outside.
flashcard_questions.q: Why are alpha sources particularly dangerous if contamination occurs inside the body?

flashcard_questions.a: James Chadwick, in 1932.
flashcard_questions.q: Who discovered the neutron and when?

glossary_terms.definition: An early model of the atom as a tiny, solid, indivisible sphere — the starting point of atomic theory in the 19th century.
Thomson's model of the atom as a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons embedded throughout, like plums in a Christmas pudding.
The model in which an atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, with electrons orbiting at much larger distances — almost all of the atom is empty space.
A subatomic particle found in the nucleus that has no electrical charge and a relative mass of 1.
Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons — and therefore different mass numbers.
An unstable nucleus that spontaneously emits radiation in order to reach a more stable state.

Alpha particles (helium nuclei) are the most ionising but least penetrating radiation; beta particles (electrons) are moderately ionising; gamma rays (electromagnetic waves) are the least ionising but most penetrating.
The time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei in a sample — or its activity — to fall to half the original value.
The unwanted deposit of radioactive material on or inside the body, which continues to emit radiation even after the source is removed from proximity.
Exposure to radiation from an external source; once the source is removed, exposure ceases.

lessons.title: Using Radioactive Materials Safely
lessons.description: Medical and industrial uses, exposure dose and radioactive waste.
lessons.content_html:
Irradiation and Contamination

Radioactive materials emit ionising radiation, which can damage living cells. Scientists and regulators distinguish carefully between two different types of exposure, because the health risks are quite different.

Irradiation occurs when a person is exposed to radiation from an external source — for example, standing near a radioactive sample that emits gamma rays. The body receives a dose, but no radioactive material enters it. Crucially, once the source is taken away, the exposure ends straight away.

Contamination is far more dangerous. Here, radioactive material gets onto or inside the body — swallowed, inhaled, or absorbed through the skin. Because the source stays close to body cells, it continues to irradiate them until it is removed or decays away. Alpha emitters are particularly hazardous as contaminants: alpha particles cause intense ionisation over a very short range, so they do serious localised damage to tissue once inside the body, even though they cannot penetrate skin from outside.

Key Fact

Irradiation = external source, exposure stops when source is removed. Contamination = radioactive material in or on the body, exposure continues. Contamination is more hazardous because the source cannot easily be removed.

Radiation and Health Risks

Ionising radiation can kill cells outright or damage DNA within them. Damaged DNA that is not repaired may lead to cancer. The severity of the risk depends on three factors: the type of radiation (its ionising ability), the half-life of the isotope (how long the source remains active), and whether the exposure is irradiation or contamination.

Alpha radiation has the highest ionising ability but the lowest penetrating power — stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper. Beta particles penetrate a few millimetres of aluminium. Gamma rays require several centimetres of lead or thick concrete to be significantly reduced. This means an alpha source is safe to handle externally if kept at arm's length, but catastrophic if inhaled — while a gamma source poses an external irradiation risk even from a distance.

Decisions about using ionising radiation in medicine always involve weighing risks against benefits. Background radiation — from cosmic rays, rocks, food, and medical procedures — means everyone receives a small annual dose. The question regulators ask is not “is there any risk?” but “is the benefit worth the risk?”

For a cancer patient, the benefit of destroying a tumour with targeted radiation may far outweigh the small extra risk of triggering a secondary cancer. A healthy person undergoing a routine scan faces a much smaller benefit, so lower-dose techniques or alternatives (such as ultrasound) are preferred. This risk–benefit reasoning underpins how regulators licence the use of radioactive materials in healthcare and industry.

Medical Uses of Radioactive Materials

Ionising radiation has two broad medical uses: imaging the inside of the body, and destroying unwanted tissue such as tumours.

A PET scan uses a radioactive tracer that emits positrons (beta-plus particles). When a positron meets an electron in body tissue, both annihilate to produce two gamma rays travelling in opposite directions. Detectors arranged around the patient pick up these paired gamma rays and use them to build a three-dimensional map of where the tracer is concentrating. PET scans are particularly valuable for detecting cancer spread and assessing brain activity, because the tracer is typically a glucose analogue that accumulates in metabolically active tissue.

Radiotherapy exploits the cell-killing power of ionising radiation. A beam of gamma radiation is directed at a tumour from several angles, all focused on the same point. This ensures the tumour receives a high dose while surrounding healthy tissue receives a lower, more manageable dose from each individual beam.

Key Fact

PET scans use a positron-emitting tracer. Positrons annihilate with electrons to produce paired gamma rays, which external detectors pick up. Radiotherapy uses a focused gamma beam to destroy tumour cells, crossing the body from multiple angles.

Background Radiation

Background radiation is the low-level radiation everyone is exposed to constantly. Sources include radon gas seeping from granite rocks, cosmic rays from space, small amounts of radioactive isotopes in food and water, and radiation from medical procedures. The level varies with location — areas with granite geology, for example, have higher radon concentrations. This background level is the baseline against which risks from additional radiation sources are judged.

Nuclear fission occurs when a slow-moving neutron is absorbed by a large, unstable nucleus — typically uranium-235 or plutonium-239. The nucleus splits into two smaller “daughter” nuclei of roughly equal size, releasing energy as kinetic energy of those particles and as gamma radiation.

The split also releases two or three additional neutrons. These can go on to trigger further fission events in nearby nuclei — a chain reaction. In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is controlled so that on average exactly one neutron from each fission causes the next fission, maintaining a steady rate of energy release. Control rods made of neutron-absorbing material regulate this.

Nuclear fusion is the process that powers stars including our Sun. Two hydrogen nuclei are forced close enough together that the strong nuclear force overcomes their electrostatic repulsion, and they fuse into a helium nucleus. In doing so, some mass is converted into energy — a very large amount of energy relative to the mass involved.

Fusion does not produce long-lived radioactive waste in the same way fission does, and its fuel (hydrogen isotopes) is far more abundant than uranium. For these reasons, controlled fusion is an active area of international research, though achieving the extreme temperatures needed to sustain fusion reactions on Earth remains a major engineering challenge.

Key Fact

Fission: a large nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) splits after absorbing a neutron, releasing energy and more neutrons that can sustain a chain reaction. Fusion: two small nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) join together, releasing large amounts of energy. Both release energy from the nuclear store.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In ‘evaluate the use of ionising radiation’ questions, always address both sides: a specific benefit (e.g. PET scan maps tumour spread) AND a specific risk (e.g. gamma irradiation may damage healthy tissue). Answers that only list one side score half the marks. Distinguish contamination from irradiation precisely — the key phrase is “the source remains in contact with the body.” For fission chain-reaction questions, state that on average one neutron per fission causes the next event; saying “all neutrons” cause further fissions describes an uncontrolled bomb, not a reactor.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Irradiation = exposure to an external source; contamination = radioactive material in or on the body and therefore more dangerous because it cannot simply be removed.
  • Medical uses of radiation include PET scanning (positron-emitting tracer maps metabolic activity via paired gamma rays) and radiotherapy (focused gamma beam destroys tumour cells).
  • Nuclear fission splits a large nucleus with a neutron, releasing energy and further neutrons that may cause a chain reaction; nuclear fusion joins two light nuclei to form a heavier one, releasing even greater energy per unit mass.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between irradiation and contamination, and explain why contamination by an alpha-emitting isotope is considered more hazardous than irradiation by the same source.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear distinction — irradiation is external exposure that stops when the source is removed; contamination means radioactive material is in/on the body and continues to emit radiation (1). Alpha particles are highly ionising (1) but have very short range, so external alpha poses little risk to internal organs; if inhaled/ingested, alpha causes intense localised damage to surrounding tissue (1). Any relevant link to half-life of isotope determining duration of internal dose (1). Secure: Two valid points with some comparison. Developing: One correct distinction or one hazard point. Emerging: Vague or confused answer.

practice_questions.text: A hospital uses a PET scanner to detect the spread of cancer. Describe how a PET scan produces an image, including the type of radiation used and how the scanner detects it.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Patient is given a tracer that emits positrons / beta-plus particles (1). Positrons annihilate with electrons in tissue, producing two gamma rays in opposite directions (1). External detectors on both sides record the paired gamma rays and build a 3-D image of tracer concentration (1). Secure: Two valid stages. Developing: One stage correct. Emerging: Simply names PET without mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a long half-life makes a radioactive contaminant more dangerous than a short half-life contaminant, even if both initially have the same activity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Long half-life means the number of radioactive nuclei decreases slowly (1), so activity remains significant inside the body for a prolonged period (1), leading to a larger total radiation dose to surrounding tissue over time (1). Secure: Two linked points. Developing: States long half-life = stays longer, but does not link to dose. Emerging: Vague statement about danger.

practice_questions.text: A radiotherapy machine delivers a gamma-ray beam to a tumour from six different directions, all aimed at the same point. Explain why this multi-beam approach is used rather than a single beam.
practice_questions.marks: Each individual beam passes through different healthy tissue (1) so each region of healthy tissue receives a lower dose; the tumour receives the combined dose from all six beams and is more effectively destroyed (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during nuclear fission of uranium-235 and explain how this process can be made self-sustaining in a controlled nuclear reactor.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A slow neutron is absorbed by uranium-235 nucleus (1); nucleus splits into two smaller daughter nuclei of roughly equal mass (1); releases kinetic energy of particles and gamma radiation (1); two or three neutrons are also released (1); in a reactor, control rods absorb excess neutrons so on average exactly one neutron per fission triggers the next event, maintaining a steady chain reaction (1); this controlled chain reaction releases energy at a constant rate for electricity generation (1). Secure: Four to five points with coherent explanation of chain reaction control. Developing: Describes fission but limited chain-reaction detail. Emerging: Names fission without describing the process.

practice_questions.text: A radioactive tracer used in a PET scan has a half-life of 110 minutes. A patient is given a dose at 9:00 am. Calculate how many half-lives will have passed by 3:40 pm and determine what fraction of the original activity remains at that time. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks: Time elapsed = 3:40 pm − 9:00 am = 6 hours 40 minutes = 400 minutes (1). Number of half-lives = 400 ÷ 110 = 3.636... ≈ 3.64 half-lives (1). For a clean integer check: 3 half-lives = 330 min; fraction remaining after 3 full half-lives = 1/8 (accept any correct working for partial half-lives). Award full marks for consistent method: fraction = (0.5)^(400/110) ≈ 0.079 (1). Correct final fraction stated with units or as a decimal (1). Note: both approaches (exact or integer approximation with clear working) are acceptable.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of radiation causes the greatest risk if a radioactive source is swallowed?
options: Gamma rays, because they have the greatest penetrating power
Alpha particles, because they are the most ionising at short range
Beta particles, because they can penetrate skin easily
All three cause equal risk when inside the body

knowledge_checks.q: In a PET scan, what does the scanner detect?
options: Alpha particles emitted by the tracer
Beta particles emitted directly by the tracer
Paired gamma rays produced when positrons annihilate electrons

knowledge_checks.q: Irradiation differs from contamination because irradiation stops as soon as the _____ is removed.
In nuclear fission of uranium-235, a slow-moving neutron is absorbed by the nucleus, which then splits into two smaller nuclei and releases further _____ that can trigger a chain reaction.
Match each term to its correct description.
right: Low-level radiation always present in the environment
Radioactive material in or on the body continuing to emit radiation
Joining two light nuclei to form a heavier one, releasing energy

glossary_terms.definition: Radiation from unstable nuclei — alpha particles, beta particles or gamma rays — that can ionise atoms it passes through.
Exposure to radiation from a source outside the body; exposure stops immediately when the source is removed.
When radioactive material enters or is deposited on the body, continuing to emit radiation from within or on the surface.
Positron Emission Tomography — a medical imaging technique that uses a short-lived positron emitter to map metabolic activity inside the body.
Treatment that uses ionising radiation, typically a focused gamma beam, to destroy cancer cells.
Low-level radiation from natural and artificial sources always present in the environment.
The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei after absorbing a neutron, releasing energy and further neutrons.
A self-sustaining series of fission events in which neutrons released by one fission trigger further fissions in nearby nuclei.
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing large amounts of energy.
Uncontrolled division of cells caused by damage to the DNA that controls the cell cycle; can result from radiation exposure.
